Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
The afternoon light in the displacement camp had already turned the color of rust when the convoy stalled near the border checkpoint. David Nguyen was coordinating the distribution of medical tents when the first explosion tore through the perimeter. The heat followed instantly, carrying the acrid bite of burning rubber and the sharp, medicinal tang of alcohol-based sterilizers rupturing from the supply crates. At 4:32 p.m., David made a split-second choice to secure the heavy equipment and move it to higher ground, a decision that meant leaving the makeshift triage area exposed to the advancing smoke. He tells himself it was protocol, but when the memory surfaces, it drops him into the exact physicality of that moment without any warning. He feels the searing air on his skin, hears the crackle of the burning tents, and is certain that the ground is tilting beneath him. When the event plays through his mind now, a heavy wave of shame follows, a quiet but relentless certainty that he moved in ways that contradicted everything he believed about himself as a man who protects. Since returning stateside, David had come to believe that time itself had become a threshold. Every day at 4:30 p.m., his chest tightens, his breath shallow, even when he is nowhere near a conflict zone. He started leaving his apartment early in the afternoons, avoiding the quiet hours when the memories felt most likely to break through. The habit formed slowly over weeks, then solidified into something rigid. He stopped staying in the city for evening performances. At the dance studio where he teaches and rehearses, the afternoon classes now feel like minefields. The stage manager’s routine use of industrial alcohol wipes to clean the wooden floor triggers a sudden, involuntary flinch. David finds himself holding his breath, stepping back from the work area, his mind certain that he is losing his grip on his own responses. He has told himself that his hesitation, his inability to push through the discomfort, proves he is a lousy coper. What frightens him most is the quiet realization that he cannot rely on himself to stay grounded when the smell of burnt dust from the studio’s old ventilation system seeps through the vents. He began taking the stairs instead of the elevator, skipping the main rehearsal hall entirely, and instructing his dancers to work through the sequences without him. The studio, once his sanctuary, had become a place where his own reactions seemed to betray him at every turn. Over the months, the avoidance reshaped his work and his home life. He began arriving early and leaving before the scheduled wrap, citing fatigue, though the truth was that the late afternoon hours had become unbearable. During a final dress rehearsal for a community production, the overhead stage lights grew hot, casting the familiar scent of heated metal and dust through the studio. David stepped off the floor mid-choreography, unable to continue, and left his shoes by the door. His wife, Elena, had noticed the growing distance in his eyes, the way he flinched when she poured wine or when the evening news played. She asked him to see someone, not as an ultimatum, but as an offering. David sat in the therapist’s office yesterday with his hands folded tightly in his lap, the memory of that checkpoint burning behind his ribs. He does not know if he can return to the stage or to the man he used to be, but he is hoping, quietly, that someone might help him understand why time, smell, and memory have become so heavy to carry.
